title: SPIN: Image Immunization Against Diffusion Editing via Single-Step Projection in Stochastic Neighborhoods

paper.title: SPIN: Image Immunization Against Diffusion Editing via Single-Step Projection in Stochastic Neighborhoods
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models have greatly advanced instruction-guided image editing, while also raising concerns about unauthorized image manipulation. Image immunization addresses this risk by adding imperceptible perturbations to an input image to disrupt subsequent edits. Since editing requests are unknown at image release, protection should remain effective beyond the instruction used to construct the perturbation. Existing immunization methods either require costly full-trajectory backpropagation or use intermediate objectives whose effects may be weakened by subsequent denoising. Meanwhile, a single inference path provides limited feedback about alternative denoising continuations. To address these challenges, we propose SPIN , a framework for image immunization via one-step projection over local stochastic trajectory neighborhoods. Starting from an early denoising state, SPIN generates stochastic neighboring states under the same instruction and predicts their clean latents through one-step projection without full unrolling. We then optimize a bounded input perturbation to maximize the average deviation of these predictions from a clean-edit reference, encouraging the perturbation to disrupt multiple possible editing outcomes. Experiments on two image editors demonstrate substantial gains in protection performance, with SPIN outperforming compared methods across all six metrics under seen instructions and in the more challenging unseen instruction setting.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Instruction-guided diffusion models have made it possible to modify a source image using natural-language instructions while preserving content unrelated to the requested changes ( Brooks et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Publicly available image editing models have substantially lowered the barriers to personalized image manipulation. However, the same accessibility also makes publicly released images vulnerable to unauthorized editing, which may compromise personal privacy and reputation or facilitate misleading content. Deepfake detection ( Rossler et al., 2019 ) and AI-generated image detection ( Ojha et al., 2023 ) can identify manipulated content, but operate only after such content has been produced. This motivates proactive protection that is embedded imperceptibly in images before release. Image immunization protects source images by adding imperceptible perturbations that disrupt subsequent unauthorized edits. A direct approach optimizes perturbations against the final editing output, but backpropagation through the denoising trajectory incurs substantial computational cost ( Salman et al., 2023 ) . More efficient alternatives construct surrogate objectives from denoising predictions or intermediate representations ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Liang and Wu, 2023 ) . Such objectives can target encoder representations ( Xue et al., 2024 ) , instruction-related cross-attention ( Lo et al., 2024 ) , or early denoising states ( Choi et al., 2025 ) , providing protection signals through shorter gradient paths. Nevertheless, deviations induced by intermediate representations may be attenuated by subsequent denoising, weakening their effect on the final edit. Protection under a fixed editing instruction may also depend on the specific sampling trajectory. This dependence becomes particularly relevant when future editing requests are unknown, as a single trajectory offers limited feedback about other possible continuations. The challenge is therefore to construct an effective optimization signal that reflects the perturbation’s impact on editing outcomes across multiple possible continuations, enabling protection beyond the original editing instruction. We address this challenge by proposing SPIN (Single-step Projection in Stochastic Neighborhoods), an image-immunization framework that uses predicted editing outcomes to guide protective perturbations. Single-step projection predicts a clean latent from an early denoising state. The discrepancy between this prediction and a fixed clean-edit reference provides an effective surrogate for optimizing perturbations that disrupt the final editing output. To extend this signal beyond a single inference path, SPIN generates neighboring candidate states through stochastic transitions from a shared early state. We then optimize a bounded input perturbation to maximize the average discrepancy between their projected outcomes and the reference, reducing dependence on a single construction path and promoting generalization to unseen editing instructions. Experiments on SD3 and InstructPix2Pix show that SPIN outperforms all baselines across six metrics under both seen and unseen editing instructions. Immunization success rates reach 90% and 94% under seen instructions (85% and 91% under unseen instructions), consistently exceeding those of competing methods. Ablations demonstrate that single-step projection provides an effective protection signal, while stochastic neighborhood sampling further improves generalization over single-candidate projection. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose SPIN , an image-immunization framework that uses single-step projection to guide perturbation optimization with predicted editing outcomes, providing an effective signal for disrupting the final edit. • We introduce stochastic neighborhood optimization to construct a single perturbation that targets multiple possible continuations of the editing process. By driving their projected outcomes away from the clean-edit reference, this strategy promotes disruption across different inference paths and improves generalization to unseen editing instructions. • Experiments under standard editing pipelines show that SPIN consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines in immunization success rate under both seen and unseen instructions, across flow-matching and noise-prediction diffusion editors.

sections.heading: 2.1 Instruction-Guided Diffusion Image Editing
sections.text: Diffusion models support image editing by combining a generative prior with a source image and user-specified control. SDEdit ( Meng et al., 2022 ) perturbs and denoises an input through a stochastic differential equation to balance faithfulness and realism. Later methods introduced more explicit semantic control. Prompt-to-Prompt ( Hertz et al., 2023 ) manipulates cross-attention maps to preserve spatial layout while changing textual content, whereas Imagic ( Kawar et al., 2023 ) optimizes a text embedding and fine-tunes the model for semantic edits on a single image. InstructPix2Pix ( Brooks et al., 2023 ) establishes a supervised learning paradigm for directly following natural-language editing instructions without per-image inversion or fine-tuning. UltraEdit ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) advances this paradigm through large-scale editing supervision with diverse instructions, real-image anchors, and region annotations, supporting the adaptation of pretrained generative models, including Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , to instruction-guided image editing. These advances improve the capability and accessibility of image editing, while also exposing publicly released images to increasingly diverse unauthorized transformations.

sections.heading: 2.2 Adversarial Examples
sections.text: Norm-bounded adversarial perturbations can alter model predictions ( Goodfellow et al., 2015 ) , and projected-gradient methods ( Madry et al., 2018 ) formulate their construction as constrained optimization. To improve cross-model transferability, MI-FGSM ( Dong et al., 2018 ) stabilizes updates through momentum, while VMI-FGSM ( Wang and He, 2021 ) further refines them using neighborhood gradient information. EOT ( Athalye et al., 2018 ) averages attack objectives over input transformations to improve transformation robustness, whereas universal adversarial perturbations generalize across images ( Moosavi-Dezfooli et al., 2017 ) . SPIN targets the generation trajectories of diffusion editors, optimizing a bounded input perturbation over local stochastic continuations to disrupt generation and drive final editing outputs away from their clean counterparts.

sections.heading: 2.3 Image Immunization Against Diffusion Editing
sections.text: Image immunization methods mainly differ in the optimization signal used to construct protective perturbations. PhotoGuard exposes the central trade-off through an efficient encoder-targeting objective (PhotoGuard-E) and a more output-related but expensive full-diffusion objective (PhotoGuard-D) ( Salman et al., 2023 ) . AdvDM optimizes the diffusion denoising loss, while MIST combines semantic and textural objectives to disrupt the generation process at multiple representation levels ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Liang and Wu, 2023 ) . Subsequent methods shorten the gradient path by targeting specific internal components: SDS ( Xue et al., 2024 ) applies score distillation at the vulnerable VAE bottleneck, EditShield ( Chen et al., 2024 ) shifts instruction-conditioned latent representations, and SA ( Lo et al., 2024 ) disrupts prompt-relevant cross-attention features. DiffusionGuard ( Choi et al., 2025 ) places its objective at early denoising stages. Other approaches improve complementary aspects of protection: DCT-Shield ( Bala et al., 2025 ) optimizes frequency-domain perturbations for visual fidelity and JPEG resistance, whereas SIFM ( Dong et al., 2025 ) combines intermediate-feature manipulation with semantic and perceptual criteria for evaluating edit failure. Despite their different targets, these methods either require costly differentiation through the diffusion trajectory or rely on internal surrogates whose deviations may be attenuated during subsequent denoising.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We present an image-immunization framework, termed Single-step Projection in Stochastic Neighborhoods ( SPIN ), for protecting images against unauthorized editing. To efficiently obtain a protection signal that reflects the perturbation’s effect on the predicted edit, we use single-step projection to estimate the clean latent from an intermediate denoising state. We further optimize the perturbation over a local stochastic neighborhood to reduce dependence on a single inference path and promote generalization across editing instructions.

sections.heading: 3.1 Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
sections.text: Given a source image x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] H × W × 3 x\in[0,1]^{H\times W\times 3} and an editing instruction c c , a frozen editor 𝒢 θ \mathcal{G}_{\theta} produces an edited image y = 𝒢 θ ​ ( x , c , ω ) y=\mathcal{G}_{\theta}(x,c;\omega) , where ω \omega denotes the sampling randomness. The editor iteratively denoises a latent state z t z_{t} conditioned on x x and c c , then decodes the final latent into y y . Image immunization seeks a bounded input perturbation that disrupts subsequent edits while preserving the source image’s appearance. The protected image is x δ = Π [ 0 , 1 ] ​ ( x + δ ) x_{\delta}=\Pi_{[0,1]}(x+\delta) , where Π [ 0 , 1 ] \Pi_{[0,1]} clips pixel values to the valid range. sections.heading: 3.2 Overall Framework
sections.text: Figure 1: Overview of SPIN . From a shared native prefix, local trajectory sampling generates neighboring candidates and one-step projection estimates their clean endpoints. These estimates guide perturbation optimization to drive editing outputs away from the fixed clean-edit reference. Our goal is to construct a bounded input perturbation that disrupts the final editing output and remains effective under unseen editing instructions. To this end, SPIN combines two modules, as shown in Figure 1 : (a) local trajectory sampling generates neighboring candidate states from a shared early state under a fixed construction instruction, providing feedback across multiple local continuations to reduce path dependence and support transfer to unseen instructions; (b) one-step projection estimates each candidate’s clean latent, enabling output-oriented evaluation without full sampling rollouts. We aggregate the projected candidates’ deviations from a fixed clean-edit reference to optimize the same input perturbation. The following subsections detail the projection, neighborhood construction, and perturbation optimization.

sections.heading: 3.6 Perturbation Optimization
sections.text: We reparameterize each candidate transition by adding a Gaussian noise term to its conditional mean. Holding the sampled noise fixed during backpropagation allows us to differentiate the projection loss with respect to the input perturbation through the candidate prediction, local transition, shared prefix, and image encoder. Throughout optimization, model parameters are frozen, and the clean reference z ref z_{\mathrm{ref}} is treated as a constant. We initialize the perturbation at zero and maximize Equation 4 using projected gradient ascent ( Madry et al., 2018 ) . Define the feasible set as 𝒞 ( x ) = { δ : ∥ δ ∥ ∞ ≤ ε , x + δ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] H × W × 3 } \mathcal{C}(x)=\{\delta:\|\delta\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon,\;x+\delta\in[0,1]^{H\times W\times 3}\} . sections.heading: Benchmark Datasets.
sections.text: We construct a benchmark of 500 samples from Pico-Banana, covering landscapes, artworks, multi-object scenes, real-world photographs, news imagery, public figures, and indoor scenes. For text-conditioned protection methods, perturbations are optimized using the original prompt associated with each image. Each sample is evaluated with its original prompt and five semantically disjoint editing instructions, resulting in 3,000 image-instruction pairs. Additional dataset and instruction details are provided in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: Editing Models and Evaluation Metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate InstructPix2Pix and Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3) as denoising-diffusion and flow-matching editors, respectively. We compare edits of clean and protected inputs using PSNR ( Wang and Bovik, 2009 ) , SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) , FSIM ( Zhang et al., 2011 ) , VIFP ( Sheikh and Bovik, 2006 ) , and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) . Lower values of the first four and higher LPIPS indicate stronger protection; the directions reverse for perturbation imperceptibility. Following SIFM ( Dong et al., 2025 ) , we report Immunization Success Rate (ISR): the fraction of protected edits with instruction failure or substantial perceptual degradation, judged by consensus of Kimi K2.5 ( Team et al., 2026 ) and Qwen3-VL ( Bai et al., 2025 ) . Higher ISR indicates stronger protection. See Appendices A.2 and D for evaluation details.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: For each image, we optimize an additive perturbation δ \delta under ∥ δ ∥ ∞ ≤ 8 / 255 \lVert\delta\rVert_{\infty}\leq 8/255 while keeping the model parameters frozen. Starting from δ = 0 \delta=0 , we perform 20 PGD steps with a step size of 1 / 255 1/255 , projecting the perturbation and clipping the protected image after each step. We use branch index j = 1 j=1 for both editors and set τ = 2 \tau=2 for InstructPix2Pix. Sampling noise is fixed during optimization. Evaluation uses unseen seeds, with clean and protected inputs sharing the same editing instruction and sampling noise. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix A.3 .

sections.heading: Generalization to Unseen Editing Instructions.
sections.text: We evaluate protection on semantically disjoint instructions excluded from perturbation optimization. Table 2 shows that SPIN achieves ISR of 85% on SD3 and 91% on InstructPix2Pix, with a larger advantage over competing methods than under original instructions. This advantage is consistent with its optimization across multiple stochastic trajectories, which reduces dependence on a single editing path and helps protection remain effective when the instruction changes.

sections.heading: Qualitative Comparison.
sections.text: Figures 3 and 3 compare source images, protected inputs and editing results. Many baseline methods mainly introduce texture-like patterns or slight color shifts, while the requested edits remain largely intact. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced SPIN to protect images against unauthorized editing by jointly considering the predicted outcomes of multiple local editing trajectories. This formulation makes output-oriented protection tractable without differentiating through the full denoising process. It also allows a protective perturbation to account for alternative continuations of an edit, rather than relying on a single construction path. Together, these ideas offer a practical direction for image immunization when future editing requests are unknown at the time of image release.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work studies image immunization against unauthorized instruction-guided image editing. Although our method employs adversarial attacks, its objective is defensive: to help image owners protect their content by applying bounded perturbations before publication, reducing the risk of unwanted manipulation. The method operates on input images while keeping the editing models frozen. The same perturbation mechanism could also be used to disrupt legitimate editing workflows. We therefore encourage its use on images that users own or are authorized to protect. Our experiments use images from Pico-Banana, and the edited examples serve to evaluate protection effectiveness. They should not be interpreted as authentic depictions of people or events.

sections.text: Section 3 describes the proposed method, and Section 4.1 summarizes the benchmark, editing models, metrics, and optimization settings. sections.heading: A.1 Benchmark Construction
sections.text: Our benchmark contains 500 samples drawn from Pico-Banana. The selected images cover landscapes, artworks, multi-object scenes, real-world photographs, news imagery, portraits of public figures, and indoor scenes. For protection methods that require textual conditioning, the original prompt associated with each image is used during perturbation optimization. At evaluation time, each image is paired with its original prompt and five additional editing instructions that are semantically disjoint from one another. The additional instructions are used only for evaluation and are not exposed during perturbation optimization. This separation tests whether the protection transfers to editing requests that differ from the optimization prompt. The resulting benchmark contains 3000 image–instruction pairs.

sections.heading: A.2 Editing Models and Metric Computation
sections.text: We evaluate protection efficacy using InstructPix2Pix and Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3), representing denoising-diffusion and flow-matching image editors, respectively. All protection methods are evaluated using the same editor configurations. For an input image x x , its protected counterpart x + δ x+\delta , an editing instruction c c , and sampling noise determined by seed s s , let 𝒢 θ ​ ( x , c , s ) and 𝒢 θ ​ ( x + δ , c , s ) \mathcal{G}_{\theta}(x,c;s)\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{G}_{\theta}(x+\delta,c;s) (8) denote the editing outputs obtained from the clean and protected inputs. sections.heading: Appendix D ISR Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: We follow the ISR protocol introduced by SIFM ( Dong et al., 2025 ) . For each evaluation sample, Kimi K2.5 and Qwen3-VL independently inspect the source image, the edited output produced from the protected image, and the editing instruction. Each evaluator returns binary judgments for two failure modes: (1) semantic mismatch, where the output does not realize the intended edit, and (2) substantial perceptual degradation, where artifacts, distortions, or other quality defects make the output unusable. A model-level verdict is positive when either failure mode is present. Let y i ( m ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i}^{(m)}\in\{0,1\} denote the verdict of evaluator m m for the i i -th editing attempt, where 1 indicates successful immunization. Following SIFM’s strict agreement rule, the aggregated verdict is y i = y i ( Kimi ) ​ y i ( Qwen ) . y_{i}=y_{i}^{(\mathrm{Kimi})}\,y_{i}^{(\mathrm{Qwen})}. (20) Thus, an attempt is counted as successfully immunized only when both evaluators return positive verdicts; disagreements and jointly negative verdicts are counted as failures. The evaluators are queried independently using the same judging prompt and input presentation and do not observe each other’s outputs. For N N evaluated attempts, we compute ISR = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N y i . \mathrm{ISR}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}y_{i}. (21) Higher ISR therefore indicates that a larger fraction of editing attempts are jointly judged to violate the instruction or exhibit substantial perceptual degradation.

sections.heading: System prompt.
sections.text: Both evaluators use the following system-prompt template. We replace {instruction} with the editing instruction for each attempt and provide the original, unprotected image as Image 1 and the edited result obtained from its protected version as Image 2. The doubled braces in the template become literal JSON braces after string formatting. Each evaluator returns YES or NO for semantic_mismatch and quality_degradation ; a YES for either field yields a positive model-level verdict. ⬇ JUDGE_PROMPT = """ Edit instruction : "{ instruction }" Image 1: the original image ( before editing ). Image 2: the edited result ( after applying the edit instruction to a protected / immunized version of the original image ). Judge two criteria : - semantic_mismatch : Does Image 2 FAIL to follow the edit instruction compared to Image 1? ( YES / NO ) - quality_degradation : Does Image 2 have severe artifacts / noise / distortion making it unusable ? ( YES / NO ) Do not think or explain . Reply with ONLY this JSON , no other text : {{" semantic_mismatch ":" YES or NO "," quality_degradation ":" YES or NO "}}"""

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.06334v1 [cs.CV] 05 Oct 2026 SPIN: Image Immunization Against Diffusion Editing via Single-Step Projection in Stochastic Neighborhoods Fengming Gu Affiliation: School of Advanced Interdisciplinary Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: gufengming18@mails.ucas.ac.cn Jie Zhang Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: q.li2@imperial.ac.uk Zhongqi Wang Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: zhangjie@ict.ac.cn Qiankun Li Affiliation: Imperial College London Email: wangzhongqi23s@ict.ac.cn Shiguang Shan Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: sgshan@ict.ac.cn Xilin Chen Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: xlchen@ict.ac.cn Abstract Diffusion models have greatly advanced instruction-guided image editing, while also raising concerns about unauthorized image manipulation. Image immunization addresses this risk by adding imperceptible perturbations to an input image to disrupt subsequent edits. Since editing requests are unknown at image release, protection should remain effective beyond the instruction used to construct the perturbation. Existing immunization methods either require costly full-trajectory backpropagation or use intermediate objectives whose effects may be weakened by subsequent denoising. Meanwhile, a single inference path provides limited feedback about alternative denoising continuations. To address these challenges, we propose SPIN , a framework for image immunization via one-step projection over local stochastic trajectory neighborhoods. Starting from an early denoising state, SPIN generates stochastic neighboring states under the same instruction and predicts their clean latents through one-step projection without full unrolling. We then optimize a bounded input perturbation to maximize the average deviation of these predictions from a clean-edit reference, encouraging the perturbation to disrupt multiple possible editing outcomes. Experiments on two image editors demonstrate substantial gains in protection performance, with SPIN outperforming compared methods across all six metrics under seen instructions and in the more challenging unseen instruction setting. 1 Introduction Instruction-guided diffusion models have made it possible to modify a source image using natural-language instructions while preserving content unrelated to the requested changes ( Brooks et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Publicly available image editing models have substantially lowered the barriers to personalized image manipulation. However, the same accessibility also makes publicly released images vulnerable to unauthorized editing, which may compromise personal privacy and reputation or facilitate misleading content. Deepfake detection ( Rossler et al., 2019 ) and AI-generated image detection ( Ojha et al., 2023 ) can identify manipulated content, but operate only after such content has been produced. This motivates proactive protection that is embedded imperceptibly in images before release. Image immunization protects source images by adding imperceptible perturbations that disrupt subsequent unauthorized edits. A direct approach optimizes perturbations against the final editing output, but backpropagation through the denoising trajectory incurs substantial computational cost ( Salman et al., 2023 ) . More efficient alternatives construct surrogate objectives from denoising predictions or intermediate representations ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Liang and Wu, 2023 ) . Such objectives can target encoder representations ( Xue et al., 2024 ) , instruction-related cross-attention ( Lo et al., 2024 ) , or early denoising states ( Choi et al., 2025 ) , providing protection signals through shorter gradient paths. Nevertheless, deviations induced by intermediate representations may be attenuated by subsequent denoising, weakening their effect on the final edit. Protection under a fixed editing instruction may also depend on the specific sampling trajectory. This dependence becomes particularly relevant when future editing requests are unknown, as a single trajectory offers limited feedback about other possible continuations. The challenge is therefore to construct an effective optimization signal that reflects the perturbation’s impact on editing outcomes across multiple possible continuations, enabling protection beyond the original editing instruction. We address this challenge by proposing SPIN (Single-step Projection in Stochastic Neighborhoods), an image-immunization framework that uses predicted editing outcomes to guide protective perturbations. Single-step projection predicts a clean latent from an early denoising state. The discrepancy between this prediction and a fixed clean-edit reference provides an effective surrogate for optimizing perturbations that disrupt the final editing output. To extend this signal beyond a single inference path, SPIN generates neighboring candidate states through stochastic transitions from a shared early state. We then optimize a bounded input perturbation to maximize the average discrepancy between their projected outcomes and the reference, reducing dependence on a single construction path and promoting generalization to unseen editing instructions. Experiments on SD3 and InstructPix2Pix show that SPIN outperforms all baselines across six metrics under both seen and unseen editing instructions. Immunization success rates reach 90% and 94% under seen instructions (85% and 91% under unseen instructions), consistently exceeding those of competing methods. Ablations demonstrate that single-step projection provides an effective protection signal, while stochastic neighborhood sampling further improves generalization over single-candidate projection. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose SPIN , an image-immunization framework that uses single-step projection to guide perturbation optimization with predicted editing outcomes, providing an effective signal for disrupting the final edit. • We introduce stochastic neighborhood optimization to construct a single perturbation that targets multiple possible continuations of the editing process. By driving their projected outcomes away from the clean-edit reference, this strategy promotes disruption across different inference paths and improves generalization to unseen editing instructions. • Experiments under standard editing pipelines show that SPIN consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines in immunization success rate under both seen and unseen instructions, across flow-matching and noise-prediction diffusion editors. 2 Related Work 2.1 Instruction-Guided Diffusion Image Editing Diffusion models support image editing by combining a generative prior with a source image and user-specified control. SDEdit ( Meng et al., 2022 ) perturbs and denoises an input through a stochastic differential equation to balance faithfulness and realism. Later methods introduced more explicit semantic control. Prompt-to-Prompt ( Hertz et al., 2023 ) manipulates cross-attention maps to preserve spatial layout while changing textual content, whereas Imagic ( Kawar et al., 2023 ) optimizes a text embedding and fine-tunes the model for semantic edits on a single image. InstructPix2Pix ( Brooks et al., 2023 ) establishes a supervised learning paradigm for directly following natural-language editing instructions without per-image inversion or fine-tuning. UltraEdit ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) advances this paradigm through large-scale editing supervision with diverse instructions, real-image anchors, and region annotations, supporting the adaptation of pretrained generative models, including Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , to instruction-guided image editing. These advances improve the capability and accessibility of image editing, while also exposing publicly released images to increasingly diverse unauthorized transformations. 2.2 Adversarial Examples Norm-bounded adversarial perturbations can alter model predictions ( Goodfellow et al., 2015 ) , and projected-gradient methods ( Madry et al., 2018 ) formulate their construction as constrained optimization. To improve cross-model transferability, MI-FGSM ( Dong et al., 2018 ) stabilizes updates through momentum, while VMI-FGSM ( Wang and He, 2021 ) further refines them using neighborhood gradient information. EOT ( Athalye et al., 2018 ) averages attack objectives over input transformations to improve transformation robustness, whereas universal adversarial perturbations generalize across images ( Moosavi-Dezfooli et al., 2017 ) . SPIN targets the generation trajectories of diffusion editors, optimizing a bounded input perturbation over local stochastic continuations to disrupt generation and drive final editing outputs away from their clean counterparts. 2.3 Image Immunization Against Diffusion Editing Image immunization methods mainly differ in the optimization signal used to construct protective perturbations. PhotoGuard exposes the central trade-off through an efficient encoder-targeting objective (PhotoGuard-E) and a more output-related but expensive full-diffusion objective (PhotoGuard-D) ( Salman et al., 2023 ) . AdvDM optimizes the diffusion denoising loss, while MIST combines semantic and textural objectives to disrupt the generation process at multiple representation levels ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Liang and Wu, 2023 ) . Subsequent methods shorten the gradient path by targeting specific internal components: SDS ( Xue et al., 2024 ) applies score distillation at the vulnerable VAE bottleneck, EditShield ( Chen et al., 2024 ) shifts instruction-conditioned latent representations, and SA ( Lo et al., 2024 ) disrupts prompt-relevant cross-attention features. DiffusionGuard ( Choi et al., 2025 ) places its objective at early denoising stages. Other approaches improve complementary aspects of protection: DCT-Shield ( Bala et al., 2025 ) optimizes frequency-domain perturbations for visual fidelity and JPEG resistance, whereas SIFM ( Dong et al., 2025 ) combines intermediate-feature manipulation with semantic and perceptual criteria for evaluating edit failure. Despite their different targets, these methods either require costly differentiation through the diffusion trajectory or rely on internal surrogates whose deviations may be attenuated during subsequent denoising. 3 Method We present an image-immunization framework, termed Single-step Projection in Stochastic Neighborhoods ( SPIN ), for protecting images against unauthorized editing. To efficiently obtain a protection signal that reflects the perturbation’s effect on the predicted edit, we use single-step projection to estimate the clean latent from an intermediate denoising state. We further optimize the perturbation over a local stochastic neighborhood to reduce dependence on a single inference path and promote generalization across editing instructions. 3.1 Preliminaries and Problem Formulation Given a source image x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] H × W × 3 x\in[0,1]^{H\times W\times 3} and an editing instruction c c , a frozen editor 𝒢 θ \mathcal{G}_{\theta} produces an edited image y = 𝒢 θ ​ ( x , c , ω ) y=\mathcal{G}_{\theta}(x,c;\omega) , where ω \omega denotes the sampling randomness. The editor iteratively denoises a latent state z t z_{t} conditioned on x x and c c , then decodes the final latent into y y . Image immunization seeks a bounded input perturbation that disrupts subsequent edits while preserving the source image’s appearance. The protected image is x δ = Π [ 0 , 1 ] ​ ( x + δ ) x_{\delta}=\Pi_{[0,1]}(x+\delta) , where Π [ 0 , 1 ] \Pi_{[0,1]} clips pixel values to the valid range. For a given instruction c c and sampling randomness ω \omega , we formulate the protection objective as: δ ⋆ = arg ⁡ max ‖ δ ‖ ∞ ≤ ε ​ ℒ ​ ( 𝒢 θ ​ ( x δ , c , ω ) , 𝒢 θ ​ ( x , c , ω ) ) , \delta^{\star}=\underset{\|\delta\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon}{\arg\max}\;\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{G}_{\theta}(x_{\delta},c;\omega),\mathcal{G}_{\theta}(x,c;\omega)\right), (1) where ε \varepsilon limits the perturbation magnitude to preserve input fidelity, and ℒ \mathcal{L} measures the discrepancy between protected and clean editing outputs. From a shared native prefix, local trajectory sampling generates neighboring candidates and one-step projection estimates their clean endpoints. These estimates guide perturbation optimization to drive editing outputs away from the fixed clean-edit reference. Our goal is to construct a bounded input perturbation that disrupts the final editing output and remains effective under unseen editing instructions. To this end, SPIN combines two modules, as shown in Figure 1 : (a) local trajectory sampling generates neighboring candidate states from a shared early state under a fixed construction instruction, providing feedback across multiple local continuations to reduce path dependence and support transfer to unseen instructions; (b) one-step projection estimates each candidate’s clean latent, enabling output-oriented evaluation without full sampling rollouts. We aggregate the projected candidates’ deviations from a fixed clean-edit reference to optimize the same input perturbation. The reference is held fixed throughout perturbation optimization, and the discrepancy is computed in the shared clean-latent space. We construct a benchmark of 500 samples from Pico-Banana, covering landscapes, artworks, multi-object scenes, real-world photographs, news imagery, public figures, and indoor scenes. For text-conditioned protection methods, perturbations are optimized using the original prompt associated with each image. Each sample is evaluated with its original prompt and five semantically disjoint editing instructions, resulting in 3,000 image-instruction pairs. Additional dataset and instruction details are provided in Appendix A.1 . Editing Models and Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate InstructPix2Pix and Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3) as denoising-diffusion and flow-matching editors, respectively. We compare edits of clean and protected inputs using PSNR ( Wang and Bovik, 2009 ) , SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) , FSIM ( Zhang et al., 2011 ) , VIFP ( Sheikh and Bovik, 2006 ) , and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) . Lower values of the first four and higher LPIPS indicate stronger protection; the directions reverse for perturbation imperceptibility. Following SIFM ( Dong et al., 2025 ) , we report Immunization Success Rate (ISR): the fraction of protected edits with instruction failure or substantial perceptual degradation, judged by consensus of Kimi K2.5 ( Team et al., 2026 ) and Qwen3-VL ( Bai et al., 2025 ) . Higher ISR indicates stronger protection. See Appendices A.2 and D for evaluation details. Implementation Details. For each image, we optimize an additive perturbation δ \delta under ∥ δ ∥ ∞ ≤ 8 / 255 \lVert\delta\rVert_{\infty}\leq 8/255 while keeping the model parameters frozen. Starting from δ = 0 \delta=0 , we perform 20 PGD steps with a step size of 1 / 255 1/255 , projecting the perturbation and clipping the protected image after each step. We use branch index j = 1 j=1 for both editors and set τ = 2 \tau=2 for InstructPix2Pix. Sampling noise is fixed during optimization. Evaluation uses unseen seeds, with clean and protected inputs sharing the same editing instruction and sampling noise. This formulation makes output-oriented protection tractable without differentiating through the full denoising process. It also allows a protective perturbation to account for alternative continuations of an edit, rather than relying on a single construction path. Together, these ideas offer a practical direction for image immunization when future editing requests are unknown at the time of image release. Ethics statement This work studies image immunization against unauthorized instruction-guided image editing. Although our method employs adversarial attacks, its objective is defensive: to help image owners protect their content by applying bounded perturbations before publication, reducing the risk of unwanted manipulation. The method operates on input images while keeping the editing models frozen. The same perturbation mechanism could also be used to disrupt legitimate editing workflows. We therefore encourage its use on images that users own or are authorized to protect. Our experiments use images from Pico-Banana, and the edited examples serve to evaluate protection effectiveness. They should not be interpreted as authentic depictions of people or events.
